exit_polls.pollster: ABC/NBC/CBS exit polls, New Jersey governor

results.vote_among_them: roughly even split (ABC); CBS: Ciattarelli won voters who said electricity was a major problem, Sherrill won economy-first voters

elections_role_of_electricity_prices.role_of_electricity_prices: Central. NJ BPU warned of 17-20% bill increases from June 1, 2025 (PJM capacity prices). Both candidates' first fall TV ads were about bills; Sherrill pledged 'Day 1... a state of emergency on utility costs... to end these rate hikes'; Ciattarelli blamed Murphy/Democrats, pledged to exit RGGI and ban offshore wind. ~6 in 10 voters called electricity costs a major problem but split about evenly between candidates.

Data centers and power bills were campaign themes (rally banner 'The Energy Bills Are Too Damn High'; at least 29 data-center bills in the 2025 General Assembly). Economy-first voters (~half) backed Spanberger by 20+ points; no VA-specific electricity exit question found. By July 2026 Spanberger's approval was 44/47 (VCU).

elections_role_of_electricity_prices.race: 2025 Georgia Public Service Commission (Districts 2 and 3, special)
elections_role_of_electricity_prices.loser: Tim Echols (R) and Fitz Johnson (R), incumbents
elections_role_of_electricity_prices.role_of_electricity_prices: Decisive. Both Democrats won ~63% (unofficial) on turnout ~30% of 2024. Georgia Power bills had risen six times in two years (~$175/month typical); Georgia Power planned ~$15B of new capacity mainly for data centers. Echols: 'The Democrats... did a good job focusing everything on that power bill.' GOP had touted a 3-year base-rate freeze.

elections_role_of_electricity_prices.winner: Peter Hubbard (D, incumbent) and Shelia Edwards (D)
elections_role_of_electricity_prices.role_of_electricity_prices: Democrats won a 3-2 PSC majority (first in about three decades). Hubbard ran on an analysis that data-center electricity discounts shift >$1B of infrastructure costs onto residential customers; Edwards: data centers 'must pay the full cost'. Even the GOP candidate said data centers should pay their fair share. Environmental groups spent >$4M.
Promised to slow data-center construction, with an executive order for a temporary moratorium on new data-center approvals; argued the buildout strains the grid and nudges bills higher.

CBS: AI data centers a major factor for over half of voters; 76% opposed a new data center in their community, and those voters went 64-34 Democratic for House. Candidates such as Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-OH) and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D-TX) made data centers central. Reason counted 41 local data-center ballot measures (mostly bans/moratoria/zoning); the anti-data-center side won all but two. Counter-signal: only ~3% named data centers the single most important issue (NBC), and Democrats who led with data centers in ads did worse than those who didn't (Reason).

Brookings: EIA average retail rates +7.1% in 2025 (DC +26.3%, PA +18.9%, RI +16.3%); candidates mostly folded power bills into a general "affordability" message rather than specific remedies (moratoria, large-load tariffs, Ratepayer Protection Pledge).

counterpoints.point: Opposition is about more than bills: in Harvard/YouGov modelling, community quality of life outweighs electricity prices ~3:1 in explaining support.
Americans blame utilities first: 64% name utilities wanting more money as a major reason vs 43% data centers (Pew, Mar 2026); CAP ranks data centers 4th.
Rules beat bans: 57% prefer rules incl. bill protections vs 23% a moratorium (Morning Consult/ARI); 61% think making tech pay lowers prices vs 48% for a moratorium (Third Way).

Rainey Center (right-leaning) polling: telling voters about the Ratepayer Protection Pledge (tech pays full grid-connection cost) raised support for AI data centers ('The public isn't opposed to data centers, they're opposed to paying for them on their power bill').
Perceived local economic benefits persist: VA voters 56% positive on job growth (WaPo-Schar); Pew finds more say mostly good than bad for local jobs and tax revenue.
